points.name: The Copyright Office is writing the rules

summary: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey places the Information sector, which covers media and related industries under NAICS 51, at 45.0% AI adoption in its latest reading, up from 41.9% in the prior period. That makes Information one of the more actively adopting sectors in the survey, reflecting how deeply generation tools have moved into editorial, audio, video, and advertising production workflows over a short span of time.

The legal environment surrounding that adoption is, however, unusually turbulent. The U.S. Copyright Office launched a formal AI initiative in early 2023, solicited public comment through a Federal Register notice of inquiry, and received more than 10,000 comments by December 2023. The Office has since been issuing its findings in sequential parts: Part 1, published July 31, 2024, addresses digital replicas and recommends a federal law governing them; Part 2, published January 29, 2025, addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI; and a pre-publication version of Part 3 was released May 9, 2025, in response to congressional pressure, with a final version to follow without substantive changes expected. These reports represent the primary legal reference for how media companies should think about what they create with AI and what they feed into it.

Parallel to the regulatory process, litigation is reshaping the commercial relationship between media rights holders and AI developers. The lawsuit tracker maintained on this site follows 102 major cases covering copyright, privacy, and safety claims, with court dockets checked daily. Active proceedings involve Perplexity AI, Runway AI, Stability AI, and others across multiple courts, and the docket activity is extensive and ongoing. Cases span training-data ingestion of news and books, image generation, and output liability, meaning that virtually every content category media companies produce is implicated somewhere in the active litigation.

For a media organization weighing deployment, the pattern the sources reveal is straightforward: adoption is already widespread across the sector, so the competitive question is less whether to use AI than how to use it within a legal framework that is still being written. The Copyright Office's multi-part study is the authoritative guidance on what can be registered, what training-data use may be permissible, and how digital replicas of real people will likely be regulated. Any organization licensing its content to AI developers or building AI into its production stack should treat Part 3 of that report and its congressional updates as required reading.

Where the sources are silent is on specific vendor market share, measured cost savings, or revenue attribution within the media sector specifically, so comparisons of ROI by tool or workflow are not supported by this material. What is clear is that the legal risk is not theoretical: the volume and recency of docket activity in the tracker, including filings as recent as August 2026, indicate that courts are actively adjudicating questions whose outcomes will determine how foundational AI agreements in media are structured for years to come.
